<div class="nv-rule" id="matching-is-not-dispatching">

## The router stops at matching: a match is a name and typed parameters, and nothing here dispatches

<div class="nv-rule-tags">
<span class="nv-rule-status" data-status="shipped">Shipped</span>
<span class="nv-rule-flag">Differs from PHP</span>
<a class="nv-rule-id" href="#matching-is-not-dispatching"><code>routing/matching-is-not-dispatching</code></a>
</div>

```php
Core\Request::route(): ?Router\Match;                                   // the match the server made
Core\Router::match(Http\Method $method, tainted string $path): ?Router\Match;
Core\Router::methodsFor(tainted string $path): array<Http\Method>;      // [] ⇒ 404, else 405 + Allow:
Core\Router::url(string $name, array<string, mixed> $params): string;         // launder (URL path)
Core\Router::urlAbsolute(string $name, array<string, mixed> $params): string; // launder (URL)
Core\Router\Match::name(): ?string;
Core\Router\Match::params(): array<tainted string|int|uint|decimal|Core\Uuid|Parses>;
Core\Router\Match::param(string $name): ?(tainted string|int|uint|decimal|Core\Uuid|Parses);
Core\Router\Match::method(): Http\Method;
Core\Router\Match::access(): ?string;                                   // the resolved name of `allow:`
```

The server matches a request once, before any application code, and `Core\Request::route()` is that
match; `match` asks the same table about a verb and a path the program chose. Either answers a name,
typed captures, the declared verb and the access decision, and **nothing invocable** — no `->invoke()`,
no callable, no class-and-method strings. Any route in the table may have matched, so a capture's type
is one union and a read is guarded by `name`: one `switch`, written by the program or generated by its
framework, in which the program states the type a capture already is with `as`. `access()` is the
decision riding on the match uninterpreted ([`security/access-is-checked-for-presence-not-meaning`](/docs/rules/security/protocols-and-tokens/#access-is-checked-for-presence-not-meaning "The compiler proves a route's access decision was written, never that it was honoured")),
as the resolved name of the constant `allow:` wrote, so a dispatcher checks it once above that `switch`
and the check covers every arm.

What the router deliberately does not do, because each is a framework opinion: **no dispatch** —
nothing calls the annotated method; **no controller convention** — no base class, naming rule or
directory layout; **no return-value-to-response rule** — what a handler returns is between it and
whoever called it; **no middleware, filters, groups or route-level rate limit**
([`core-classes/ratelimit-two-members`](/docs/rules/core-classes/codecs-sessions-and-signatures/#ratelimit-two-members "consume and shed are two jobs with two verbs, and neither is a tier of the other") declines the last for the same reason); **no
`HEAD`-implies-`GET`, no automatic `OPTIONS`, no trailing-slash normalisation** — each is somebody's
wrong default, and the server decides them above the table, visibly. A framework can build dispatch
on top, use `url` alone, or ignore all of it, and none of those choices is penalised.

Typed `callable` would not move this line: routes share no signature and handlers no return type, so
routing is not a case that forces [`types/grammar`](/docs/rules/types/declarations-and-numbers/#grammar "The type grammar is a closed set of atoms under unions and intersections")'s deferral. Signing a route's identity is
[`core-classes/router-signed-url`](/docs/rules/core-classes/codecs-sessions-and-signatures/#router-signed-url "Core\Router signs a route name and its parameters, so a signature survives a remount").

<aside class="nv-rule-diverges">
<p class="nv-rule-diverges-label">Where this differs from PHP</p>
<p>No framework router's dispatch is here — no controller base class, no middleware, no return-value-to-response rule, no <code>HEAD</code>-implies-<code>GET</code> or trailing-slash normalisation; the program or its framework writes the <code>switch</code></p>
</aside>

<div class="nv-rule" id="a-match-is-not-invocable">

## A match carries a name and typed parameters and nothing invocable, and typed `callable` would not change that

<div class="nv-rule-tags">
<span class="nv-rule-status" data-status="shipped">Shipped</span>
<span class="nv-rule-flag">Differs from PHP</span>
<a class="nv-rule-id" href="#a-match-is-not-invocable"><code>routing/a-match-is-not-invocable</code></a>
</div>

`Core\Router\Match` carries a declared name, the typed captures the path filled, the declared verb and
the access decision's name, and nothing invocable: no `->invoke()`, no callable, no class-and-method
strings, and the handler's `Class::method` label never crosses. A first-class reference to the
matched method would need `callable` to carry a signature, which [`types/grammar`](/docs/rules/types/declarations-and-numbers/#grammar "The type grammar is a closed set of atoms under unions and intersections") defers — but
routing is not a forcing case for that deferral, and typed `callable` would not remove the dispatch
`switch`, for three independent reasons.

Routes do not share a signature: `show(uint $id)`, `index()` and `blog(uint $y, uint $m, string $slug)`
cannot inhabit one `handler` field, and pre-binding the converted parameters into a zero-argument closure
is dispatch. Handlers have no common return type, and a `callable(): Response` would force one, which is
a framework opinion `Core` refuses to hold. And the boundary ground survives regardless: invoking would
be dispatch, which the table refuses on its own account
([`routing/the-servers-match-dispatches-nothing`](/docs/rules/routing/matching/#the-servers-match-dispatches-nothing "The server's match dispatches nothing, and a request the table does not claim is served by the program")).

The ergonomic cost is paid where the framework layer already sits: `Web\Controller` generates the
`switch` from the route table while compiling ([`programs/framework-web-package`](/docs/rules/programs/the-framework/#framework-web-package "The opinionated half is nvs/web, a first-party package providing the Web namespace")), and an application
declining the framework writes it itself, permanently. The roster of compiler-recognised attributes this
table draws on has one home ([`core-classes/derive-attribute`](/docs/rules/core-classes/codecs-sessions-and-signatures/#derive-attribute "One written attribute per format generates a codec, and it is matched by resolved name")), and no rule restates its size.

<aside class="nv-rule-diverges">
<p class="nv-rule-diverges-label">Where this differs from PHP</p>
<p>There is no <code>$route-&gt;getCallable()</code>; the handler is reached by a <code>switch</code> the framework generates or the application writes</p>
</aside>

<dl class="nv-rule-meta"><div class="nv-rule-meta-row"><dt>See also</dt><dd><a href="/docs/rules/routing/matching/#the-servers-match-dispatches-nothing" title="The server's match dispatches nothing, and a request the table does not claim is served by the program"><code>routing/the-servers-match-dispatches-nothing</code></a> <a href="/docs/rules/types/declarations-and-numbers/#grammar" title="The type grammar is a closed set of atoms under unions and intersections"><code>types/grammar</code></a> <a href="/docs/rules/programs/the-framework/#framework-web-package" title="The opinionated half is nvs/web, a first-party package providing the Web namespace"><code>programs/framework-web-package</code></a> <a href="/docs/rules/core-classes/codecs-sessions-and-signatures/#derive-attribute" title="One written attribute per format generates a codec, and it is matched by resolved name"><code>core-classes/derive-attribute</code></a> <a href="/docs/rules/routing/matching/#matching-is-not-dispatching" title="The router stops at matching: a match is a name and typed parameters, and nothing here dispatches"><code>routing/matching-is-not-dispatching</code></a></dd></div><div class="nv-rule-meta-row"><dt>Decided in</dt><dd><a href="https://github.com/novis-lang/novis/blob/main/docs/decisions/0102.md">record 0102</a> <a href="https://github.com/novis-lang/novis/blob/main/docs/decisions/0077.md">record 0077</a> <a href="https://github.com/novis-lang/novis/blob/main/docs/decisions/0007.md">record 0007</a> <a href="https://github.com/novis-lang/novis/blob/main/docs/decisions/0199.md">record 0199</a></dd></div></dl>

</div>

<div class="nv-rule" id="matched-once-before-the-handler">

## A request is matched once, before any application code runs, and `Core\Request::route()` is that match

<div class="nv-rule-tags">
<span class="nv-rule-status" data-status="shipped">Shipped</span>
<span class="nv-rule-flag">Differs from PHP</span>
<a class="nv-rule-id" href="#matched-once-before-the-handler"><code>routing/matched-once-before-the-handler</code></a>
</div>

The server matches the incoming request against the compiled table **once**, before any application
code runs, and records the result on the request. `Core\Request::route(): ?Core\Router\Match` returns
that match. `null` means the table claimed nothing for this method and path — or the program declared no
`#[Route]` at all, which builds no table and matches nothing. Nothing during the request can move it:
the match lives on the request carrier rather than on the context, so there is no place a second match
could be written from inside the program.

It is what three readers were written against. The CSRF check ([`security/csrf-is-on-by-default`](/docs/rules/security/protocols-and-tokens/#csrf-is-on-by-default "The server refuses an unsafe verb without a valid CSRF token, and the opt-out is written on the route itself"))
needs to know which handler a `POST` is for, the `route` metric label needs the declared name, and the
access decision rides on it uninterpreted ([`security/access-is-checked-for-presence-not-meaning`](/docs/rules/security/protocols-and-tokens/#access-is-checked-for-presence-not-meaning "The compiler proves a route's access decision was written, never that it was honoured")).
Each reads the door's answer rather than matching again, which **removes** a match for most requests
rather than adding one — a match is about a quarter of the header parse the server performs anyway.

`Core\Router::match(Http\Method, tainted string)` remains for matching some *other* verb and path the
caller chose. It takes the same walk as the door, so the two cannot disagree about one path, and an
in-process test request ([`testing/in-process-request`](/docs/rules/testing/doubles-and-the-runner/#in-process-request "A test request is dispatched in-process through the compiled route table, and its input arrives tainted")) crosses the door's match the same way.

<aside class="nv-rule-diverges">
<p class="nv-rule-diverges-label">Where this differs from PHP</p>
<p>The match is made by the server and read off the request, not by a framework kernel in userland that matches and then calls the controller</p>
</aside>

<div class="nv-rule" id="the-servers-match-dispatches-nothing">

## The server's match dispatches nothing, and a request the table does not claim is served by the program

<div class="nv-rule-tags">
<span class="nv-rule-status" data-status="shipped">Shipped</span>
<span class="nv-rule-flag">Differs from PHP</span>
<a class="nv-rule-id" href="#the-servers-match-dispatches-nothing"><code>routing/the-servers-match-dispatches-nothing</code></a>
</div>

The server computes a name and typed parameters and stops there. It never calls the annotated method,
never decides what a return value means, and never wraps anything: the route table is complete without
crossing into dispatch, and what a match *means* is the program's to decide — its own `switch`, or the
one the framework generates ([`programs/framework-web-package`](/docs/rules/programs/the-framework/#framework-web-package "The opinionated half is nvs/web, a first-party package providing the Web namespace")).

So a request the table does not claim is an ordinary served request. `route()` answers `null`, the
program runs exactly as it would for any other request, and the `404` — if it is one — is something the
program sends, not something the door refuses with. A door that refused a miss would refuse every
request of a program declaring no `#[Route]`, which is the opt-in table inverted.

The boundary holds one layer down as well. `Core\Router::match` answers a `Core\Router\Match` and
nothing invocable ([`routing/a-match-is-not-invocable`](/docs/rules/routing/matching/#a-match-is-not-invocable "A match carries a name and typed parameters and nothing invocable, and typed callable would not change that")), and the one decision the server enforces on
a match is CSRF ([`security/csrf-is-on-by-default`](/docs/rules/security/protocols-and-tokens/#csrf-is-on-by-default "The server refuses an unsafe verb without a valid CSRF token, and the opt-out is written on the route itself")) — the access name rides through for whoever
dispatches to read.

<aside class="nv-rule-diverges">
<p class="nv-rule-diverges-label">Where this differs from PHP</p>
<p>A matched route never calls anything; the program or the framework dispatches, and a <code>null</code> route is a fact the program reads rather than a 404 anything sends</p>
</aside>

<div class="nv-rule" id="a-refused-verb-is-not-a-missing-path">

## A missing path and a refused verb are different answers, and `methodsFor` is what tells them apart

<div class="nv-rule-tags">
<span class="nv-rule-status" data-status="shipped">Shipped</span>
<span class="nv-rule-flag">Differs from PHP</span>
<a class="nv-rule-id" href="#a-refused-verb-is-not-a-missing-path"><code>routing/a-refused-verb-is-not-a-missing-path</code></a>
</div>

`Core\Router::methodsFor(tainted string $path): array<Http\Method>` tells a missing path from a refused
verb. An empty array means no route claims the path at all — `404`. A non-empty one means the path
exists under other verbs — `405`, and the list is the `Allow:` header RFC 9110 requires beside it. Each
verb appears once, as a `Core\Http\Method` case, in declaration order.

It is asked only after `Core\Request::route()` or `match` has answered `null`, so a served request pays
nothing for it, and `match` keeps its two-state return rather than growing a verb list on the success
path where nobody reads it. A program with no `#[Route]` answers the empty array, because "no route
claims this path" is exactly true of it.

Where an optional trailing capture makes a node terminal
([`routing/a-trailing-segment-may-be-absent`](/docs/rules/routing/declaring-a-route/#a-trailing-segment-may-be-absent "{name?} captures one trailing segment or none, and its parameter's default is what makes the absent case well-typed")), both forms report the same verbs:
`methodsFor("/posts")` on a table declaring `/posts/{page?}` returns that route's verbs, so the shorter
form cannot `404` while the longer one `405`s. A plain `OPTIONS` is answerable by an application from
this list; the server still answers none on its behalf, because which to answer is a convention.

<aside class="nv-rule-diverges">
<p class="nv-rule-diverges-label">Where this differs from PHP</p>
<p>A wrong verb on a known path is a 405 with an <code>Allow:</code> list asked of the table, rather than the 404 a hand-rolled dispatch falls into</p>
</aside>

<dl class="nv-rule-meta"><div class="nv-rule-meta-row"><dt>See also</dt><dd><a href="/docs/rules/routing/matching/#matched-once-before-the-handler" title="A request is matched once, before any application code runs, and Core\Request::route() is that match"><code>routing/matched-once-before-the-handler</code></a> <a href="/docs/rules/routing/declaring-a-route/#a-trailing-segment-may-be-absent" title="{name?} captures one trailing segment or none, and its parameter's default is what makes the absent case well-typed"><code>routing/a-trailing-segment-may-be-absent</code></a> <a href="/docs/rules/routing/matching/#matching-is-not-dispatching" title="The router stops at matching: a match is a name and typed parameters, and nothing here dispatches"><code>routing/matching-is-not-dispatching</code></a></dd></div><div class="nv-rule-meta-row"><dt>Decided in</dt><dd><a href="https://github.com/novis-lang/novis/blob/main/docs/decisions/0102.md">record 0102</a> <a href="https://github.com/novis-lang/novis/blob/main/docs/decisions/0097.md">record 0097</a></dd></div><div class="nv-rule-meta-row"><dt>Guarded by</dt><dd><a href="https://github.com/novis-lang/novis/blob/main/tests/conformance/core/methods-for-answers-nothing-for-an-unclaimed-path-and-every-verb-for-a-claimed-one.nvst"><code>tests/conformance/core/methods-for-answers-nothing-for-an-unclaimed-path-and-every-verb-for-a-claimed-one.nvst</code></a> <a href="https://github.com/novis-lang/novis/blob/main/tests/conformance/core/both-forms-of-an-optional-capture-claim-the-same-verbs.nvst"><code>tests/conformance/core/both-forms-of-an-optional-capture-claim-the-same-verbs.nvst</code></a> <a href="https://github.com/novis-lang/novis/blob/main/tests/conformance/core/a-paths-verbs-are-answered-once-each-as-http-method-cases.nvst"><code>tests/conformance/core/a-paths-verbs-are-answered-once-each-as-http-method-cases.nvst</code></a></dd></div></dl>

</div>

<div class="nv-rule" id="a-request-reads-its-mount">

## `Core\Request::mount()` answers the prefix the door stripped and the tainted host captures, and it is never `null`

<div class="nv-rule-tags">
<span class="nv-rule-status" data-status="shipped">Shipped</span>
<span class="nv-rule-flag">Differs from PHP</span>
<a class="nv-rule-id" href="#a-request-reads-its-mount"><code>routing/a-request-reads-its-mount</code></a>
</div>

`Core\Request::mount(): Core\Request\Mount` answers the two facts about the door a request came through:
`prefix(): string` is what the mount stripped from the path before the program saw it, and
`captures(): array<tainted string>` are the mount's glob captures in order — `{1}` is `captures[0]`.
The captures are `tainted` because they came off the wire ([`security/tainted-qualifier`](/docs/rules/security/tainted-data/#tainted-qualifier "tainted is a compile-time qualifier on string, bytes and a shape of them, spellable in any declaration and erased before codegen")), so
feeding one to a query launders normally; the prefix is the deployment's own plain text. One member for
the pair, because a request holding one mount's prefix and another's captures is a bug the shape rules
out.

**`mount()` is never `null`**, where `route()` is. A request the table does not claim is an ordinary
served request, but every request that reached a program reached it *through* a mount, and a door that
strips nothing answers `""` and an empty array rather than an absence. With no request at all it
refuses, like every other reader of the class ([`security/request-state-throws-in-an-isolate`](/docs/rules/security/closed-doors/#request-state-throws-in-an-isolate "Request, server and session state throws where there is no inbound request, rather than answering empty")).

This is how one compiled table serves many tenants, and why `#[Route]` gains no `host` field: a path is
source state and a hostname is deployment state, so each lives where it changes, and the table stays
relocatable to `/ModuleA`, `/ModuleB` or `/` with no recompile. A program never derives its own prefix
from the request target.

<aside class="nv-rule-diverges">
<p class="nv-rule-diverges-label">Where this differs from PHP</p>
<p>The deployment prefix is never derived from <code>REQUEST_URI</code> or <code>SCRIPT_NAME</code>; the server hands it over, and a tenant is a mount capture rather than a <code>host</code> field on the route</p>
</aside>
